p.x:
In my family, everyone has a different job. My father is a farmer. He grows rice and vegetables, and he starts work at five o'clock every morning. My mother works in a factory that makes shoes. She doesn't earn a big salary, but she likes her boss and her colleagues.
My older brother is a taxi driver in Bangkok. He works long hours and often finishes after midnight. My sister is a student, but she also has a part-time job in an office at the weekend. My grandfather retired ten years ago. He was a teacher for forty years. Now he looks after the chickens and tells everyone what to do!

Finding your first job can feel impossible. Many companies want staff with experience, but how can you get experience if nobody will give you a job? Being unemployed for a few months after university is normal, so don't panic. Careers advisers say there are several ways to solve this problem.
First, think about the skills you already have. Maybe you organised a school event, helped in your family's shop or volunteered at a temple fair. These all show that you are reliable and can work with others. Second, don't apply for every job you see. Choose the ones that match your qualifications and interests, and write a short, clear letter for each one.
If you are invited to an interview, find out as much as you can about the company. Candidates who know about the company's products and plans always make a better impression. Finally, be patient. Your first contract may be short or the pay may be low, but if you work hard, a promotion may come sooner than you think. Remember that most successful people started at the bottom of their career ladder.

p.t: Is the Four-Day Week the Future?
p.x:
In 2022, dozens of British companies took part in a six-month trial of a four-day working week, with no reduction in pay. The results surprised many sceptics. Most firms reported that productivity stayed the same or even rose, while staff took fewer sick days. Employees said they felt less burnout, and managers noticed that team morale improved. By the end of the trial, the vast majority of companies decided to continue.
Supporters argue that a shorter week forces people to work more efficiently. Meetings become shorter, managers learn to delegate tasks, and employees do less overtime. Companies also find it easier to recruit talented workers, since a three-day weekend is a far more attractive perk than free coffee or a ping-pong table.
Nevertheless, the model does not suit every business. Hospitals, schools and restaurants cannot simply close for a day, and some entrepreneurs running small firms worry that a lighter schedule would leave them unable to compete. Critics also warn that squeezing five days of work into four could increase each employee's daily workload. In some cases, workers have had to negotiate carefully to make sure the change did not simply mean longer days. And in industries facing financial pressure, some fear that the extra cost could eventually lead to staff being made redundant.
